af: The Wakhan Corridor in the north-east is a narrow strip drawn on the map on purpose, so Russian and British lands would never touch.
ao: The Angolan desert is home to the welwitschia, a plant that grows just two leaves in its whole life and can live over a thousand years.
al: In Albanian the country is Shqipëri, a name linked to the word for eagle: Albanians call their land the country of eagles.
ae: In the mid-20th century the place where Dubai's skyscrapers now stand was sand and fishing villages, and the main trade was pearl diving.
ar: Argentina is so long that one end has hot desert and the other has glaciers you can walk right up to.
The Iguazu falls are nearly three hundred separate cascades dropping in a horseshoe on the Brazilian border.
The tango was born in the port districts of Buenos Aires.
Patagonia yields the bones of the biggest dinosaurs ever dug up anywhere.
The gauchos, Argentina's herders, drive cattle across the pampas, a huge grass plain without a single tree.
am: Armenian lavash bread is baked by slapping thin dough onto the hot wall of a tonir, an oven sunk into the ground.
aq: All the meridians meet at the South Pole, so you can walk around the flag there and cross every time zone in a few steps.
tf: Nobody lives here permanently, only researchers at the stations — but there are hundreds of thousands of penguins and seals.
au: Australia put the kangaroo and the emu on its coat of arms because neither animal can walk backwards.
The Great Barrier Reef is built by billions of tiny creatures, and it can be seen from space.
Australia is the only continent occupied by a single country.
The platypus is a mammal that lays eggs, and it lives only in Australia.
Aboriginal Australians have lived on the continent for tens of thousands of years, one of the longest unbroken cultures on Earth.
at: Legend says the pattern came from a battle: the duke's coat was soaked red except for the strip under his belt.
az: In Azerbaijan natural gas seeps out of the ground and burns for centuries, which is why it is called the land of fire.
bi: Lake Tanganyika on Burundi's border is the second deepest lake in the world, after Baikal.
be: Belgium gave the world Tintin and the Smurfs, and in Brussels comic characters are painted right onto house walls.
bj: Benin has a town called Ganvié built entirely on stilts in a lake, where people travel between houses by boat.
bf: The country's name means roughly “land of upright people”; it replaced the old colonial name in 1984.
bd: Almost all of Bangladesh lies in a river delta, so part of the country goes under water every year in the floods.
bg: Bulgarians grow whole fields of roses for rose oil — it takes thousands of blossoms to make a single drop.
bs: One Bahamian island has pigs that swim in the sea and paddle out to meet the boats.
ba: In Mostar the old bridge is so high that locals dive from it into the river — an old tradition and a real competition.
by: The Białowieża Forest is home to the wisent, Europe's heaviest wild animal, saved when almost none were left.
bz: Off the coast of Belize lies the Great Blue Hole, an almost perfectly round sea sinkhole over 300 metres across.
bo: After rain the Uyuni salt flat turns into a giant mirror, so you seem to be walking across the sky.
br: Brazil borders almost every country in South America — all of them except Chile and Ecuador.
The Amazon pours more water into the ocean than the next several largest rivers of the world combined.
Brazil is the only country in South America where Portuguese is spoken rather than Spanish.
Brasilia was built from nothing in the middle of an empty plateau in just four years; from above it looks like an aeroplane.
The Rio carnival lasts several days, and the samba schools spend the whole year preparing for it.
bn: Brunei's capital has a whole district on the water, with houses, schools and shops on stilts above the river.
bt: Bhutan measures success by Gross National Happiness and by law must keep more than half the country under forest.
bw: The Okavango River never reaches the sea — it spreads across the desert into a huge swamp full of wildlife.
cf: Savannah and forest cover nearly the whole country, and there are so many rivers that travelling by water was once easier than by road.
ca: Canada has a longer coastline than any other country: stretched out, it would wrap around the Earth several times.
Canada has more lakes than all the other countries of the world put together.
The Canada-United States border is the longest between any two countries, and not a single soldier stands on it.
Maple syrup is boiled down from sap that runs out of a cut in the trunk in spring.
In the town of Churchill polar bears walk down the streets, so cars are left unlocked in case someone needs to hide.
ch: The other square flag belongs to Vatican City. And the Red Cross symbol is the Swiss flag reversed, honouring the country where it began.
Switzerland has kept out of war for more than two hundred years and joins no military alliances.
The Gotthard tunnel runs fifty-seven kilometres under the Alps: the train goes straight through the mountain.
Switzerland has four official languages: German, French, Italian and Romansh.
Milk chocolate was invented in Switzerland: milk went into the bar to take the bitterness away.
cl: Chile is long and thin: you can drive across it in a couple of hours, but driving its length takes days.
cn: All of China uses a single time zone, even though the country is so wide that the sun rises hours later in the west.
The Great Wall was built over more than two thousand years, and it is not one wall but many separate stretches.
Paper, the compass, gunpowder and printing were all invented in China.
Giant pandas eat almost nothing but bamboo and live in the wild only in China's mountain forests.
Chinese characters do not spell out sounds, so the same text is read aloud differently in different parts of the country.
ci: Côte d'Ivoire grows more cocoa than any other country: its beans are in almost every chocolate bar.
cm: Cameroon is called “Africa in miniature”: one country holds desert, jungle, mountains and seashore.
cd: The Congo is the only big river that crosses the equator twice, so it always has water in it.
cg: Rainforest covers nearly two thirds of the country — the second largest in the world after the Amazon.
co: Colombia has the Caño Cristales river: for a few weeks a year water plants turn it red, yellow and green.
cr: Costa Rica has had no army since 1948: it was disbanded and the money went to schools and hospitals.
cu: Cuba still runs American cars from the 1950s, kept alive by decades of repairs because new ones were long impossible to buy.
cy: The word for copper in many languages comes from the name of Cyprus: the island was famous for its copper mines in ancient times.
cz: The city of Plzeň gave its name to a whole kind of beer — pilsner, now brewed all over the world.
de: Germany gave the world printing with movable type and the kindergarten — a word other languages borrowed without translating.
Some stretches of the German autobahn have no speed limit at all, though there are fewer every year.
The word rucksack comes from German: Rucken means back and Sack means bag.
A law saying what beer may be brewed from was passed in Germany in 1516, and several thousand kinds have appeared since.
The Berlin Wall divided the city for twenty-eight years; after 1989 its pieces went to museums all over the world.
dj: Lake Assal is the lowest point in Africa, and its water is several times saltier than the sea.
dk: Legend says it fell from the sky during a battle in 1219; every Nordic flag follows the Danish cross.
do: The Dominican Republic is the only country with a Bible on its flag.
dz: Algeria is the largest country in Africa, and more than four fifths of it is Sahara.
ec: The summit of Chimborazo is the farthest point from the centre of the Earth — farther than Everest, because the planet bulges at the equator.
eg: The pyramids at Giza were already ancient in Cleopatra's day: more time separates her from their building than separates us from her.
er: Asmara has kept a whole city of 1930s Italian architecture, now on the World Heritage list.
es: The columns are the Pillars of Hercules by Gibraltar, and the ribbon around them means “further beyond”.
Spain dines later than anywhere else in Europe: sitting down at ten in the evening is quite normal.
The Sagrada Familia in Barcelona has been under construction since 1882 and is still unfinished.
Spanish is the mother tongue of hundreds of millions, and most of them live not in Spain but in Mexico.
The cave of Altamira holds paintings of bison about fifteen thousand years old.
ee: Estonia was the first country in the world to let people vote in elections over the internet.
et: Ethiopia keeps its own calendar: it has thirteen months and runs about seven years behind the usual one.
fi: Finland has about 188,000 lakes — roughly one for every thirty people.
Finland has around three million saunas, nearly one for every two people.
Finnish has fifteen grammatical cases but no future tense.
In Lapland the northern lights appear on more than half of all clear winter nights.
Finnish pupils get almost no homework and sit a real exam only at the very end of school.
fj: Fiji is made of about 330 islands, but people live on only a third of them.
fk: The Falklands have many times more sheep than people — and even more penguins than sheep.
fr: The metre was first defined in France as one forty-millionth of the Earth's circumference through the poles.
France owns islands in every ocean, which gives it one of the largest sea territories in the world.
The Eiffel Tower was due to be taken down twenty years after it went up; radio saved it when an aerial was fixed to the top.
France makes over a thousand kinds of cheese — more than one for every day of the year.
The Tour de France runs for three weeks, and you can watch it from the roadside for nothing.
ga: National parks cover more than a tenth of Gabon, and elephants and hippos wander its beaches and swim in the ocean.
gb: The flag is not symmetrical: the white stripes beside the diagonals differ in width, so it can be flown upside down.
The London Underground opened in 1863, which makes it older than the motor car.
The prime meridian runs through London, and the world counts its time from there.
Britain drives on the left, as about a third of the world's countries do.
Stonehenge was raised over four thousand years ago, and some of its stones were hauled two hundred kilometres.
ge: Georgians make wine in clay qvevri buried in the ground — and have done so for about eight thousand years.
gh: Ghana was the first African colony south of the Sahara to become independent, in 1957.
gn: Three of West Africa's great rivers, the Niger among them, all rise in the mountains of Guinea.
gm: The Gambia is mainland Africa's smallest country, a narrow ribbon along both banks of its river.
gw: Off the coast lies the Bijagós archipelago, home to hippos that swim in salty sea water.
gq: It is the only country in Africa where Spanish is an official language.
gr: Greece is made of thousands of islands, but people live on fewer than three hundred of them.
The Olympic Games began in Greece almost three thousand years ago, and wars were halted while they lasted.
The Greek alphabet is the ancestor of both Latin and Cyrillic, and alpha and beta gave us the word alphabet.
The monasteries of Meteora stand on top of sheer rocks; monks and supplies used to be hauled up in a net.
The words mathematics, music, theatre and school all come from Greek.
gl: Greenland is the largest island in the world, and almost all of it lies under ice kilometres thick.
gt: The quetzal is not only the bird on the arms but also the money: Guatemalans pay in quetzales.
gy: Kaieteur Falls drops in a single sheet almost four times higher than Niagara.
hn: Honduras gets a “rain of fish”: after heavy downpours people find live fish on the ground.
hr: The necktie was invented in Croatia: the French called it cravate after the word for Croat.
ht: Haiti was the first country where enslaved people rose up, won, and founded a state of their own.
hu: Hungarian is not related to its neighbours' languages: its closest relatives are Finnish and Estonian, and even those are distant.
id: Indonesia is made of more than 17,000 islands, where hundreds of different languages are spoken.
in: India gave the world the digit zero and chess, which grew out of the ancient game of chaturanga.
India has more than twenty official languages, and a banknote gives its value in over a dozen of them.
The Taj Mahal was built as a tomb, and its white marble changes shade from dawn to dusk.
So much rain falls at Cherrapunji that people there grow bridges out of living tree roots.
India's railways carry more than twenty million people every single day.
ie: Ireland has no wild snakes: legend credits St Patrick, but really they never made it back after the Ice Age.
Ireland is called the Emerald Isle: it rains so often that the grass stays green all year round.
Halloween grew out of the Irish festival of Samhain, and the first lanterns were carved from turnips, not pumpkins.
Ireland has two official languages, Irish and English, and road signs are written in both.
The Cliffs of Moher drop almost two hundred metres straight into the ocean.
ir: The Persian new year, Nowruz, falls on the spring equinox, and the table is set with seven items whose names all start with the same letter.
iq: In Mesopotamia, where Iraq is today, the first known writing appeared — cuneiform pressed into clay tablets.
is: In Iceland almost every home is heated with hot water straight from the ground.
il: The Dead Sea is so salty that you cannot sink in it: a person floats like a cork.
it: Italy is shaped like a boot, and the island of Sicily sits at its toe like a ball.
Two other countries sit entirely inside Italy: the Vatican and San Marino.
Vesuvius buried Pompeii in ash, and the town lay hidden for seventeen centuries before it was dug out.
The tower of Pisa began to lean while it was still being built, because the ground on one side was softer.
Venice has no streets for cars: canals run between the houses, and even the ambulance arrives by boat.
jm: Jamaica is the home of reggae, and its bobsled team once went to the Winter Olympics from an island that never sees snow.
jo: The city of Petra is carved straight into rose-coloured cliffs, its temples cut from the rock over two thousand years ago.
jp: Japan has more than 6,800 islands, and its trains are so punctual that a one-minute delay counts as an incident.
Japan sits where tectonic plates meet, so it has over a thousand earthquakes a year, though nearly all are gentle.
In spring the Japanese go out to watch the cherry blossom, and the weather forecast reports where it has opened.
Japanese writing uses three different sets of characters, and all three can turn up in a single sentence.
Mount Fuji is a volcano, and it last erupted in 1707.
kz: Kazakhstan is the largest country in the world with no access to the ocean.
ke: Kenyan runners win more marathons than anyone else; many grew up in highlands over two kilometres above the sea.
kg: The forty rays are the forty tribes united by the hero Manas, whose epic is one of the longest in the world.
kh: Angkor Wat is the largest religious building in the world, put up about 900 years ago.
kr: The Korean alphabet hangul was designed so anyone could learn to read: its letters show how the mouth and tongue are shaped.
xk: This is one of Europe's youngest states: independence was declared in 2008.
kw: Kuwait is almost all desert, and much of its drinking water comes from taking the salt out of sea water.
la: Laos is the only country in Southeast Asia with no sea coast, but the Mekong runs right through it.
lb: Lebanon's cedars were already growing in the time of the pharaohs, who used them for ships and temples.
lr: A huge number of the world's ships fly the Liberian flag, because it is easier for owners to register them there.
ly: Libya is nearly all desert, and beneath it lies a vast store of ancient groundwater piped right across the country.
lk: Sri Lanka is a leading tea producer; the crop took over after disease destroyed the island's coffee plantations.
ls: Lesotho is surrounded entirely by one country, South Africa, and all of its land lies over a kilometre above sea level.
lt: Lithuania is called the land of amber — hardened resin from trees tens of millions of years old, found for centuries along the Baltic shore.
lu: Luxembourg is the world's only grand duchy, and public transport across the whole country is free.
lv: Riga claims to be the city where the first public Christmas tree was decorated.
ma: In Morocco goats climb argan trees and eat the fruit straight off the branches.
mc: Monaco is under two square kilometres: you can walk across the whole country in less than an hour.
md: Moldova has wine cellars tens of kilometres long — people drive through them by car.
mg: Nine out of ten of Madagascar's animals and plants live nowhere else: the island broke away from the mainland long ago.
mx: Legend says the Aztecs founded their city where they saw that eagle — where Mexico City stands today.
Chocolate, maize, tomatoes, chilli and vanilla all reached the world from Mexico.
Every autumn millions of monarch butterflies gather to spend the winter in Mexico's mountain forests.
Spanish is not the only language of Mexico: the state also recognises nearly seventy indigenous languages.
Beneath the Yucatan peninsula lies the scar of the asteroid strike that finished off the dinosaurs.
mk: Lake Ohrid is millions of years old and holds fish found nowhere else on Earth.
ml: Timbuktu was a city of scholars, holding tens of thousands of manuscripts — books were valued above gold.
mm: On Lake Inle fishermen row standing up with one leg, keeping their hands free for the net.
me: The country's name means “black mountain”, given by the Venetians for the dark forests on its slopes.
mn: Mongolia has roughly ten times more livestock than people, and one of the lowest population densities on Earth.
mz: It is the only flag in the world showing a Kalashnikov rifle.
mr: One of the world's longest trains runs across Mauritania: the ore train stretches more than two kilometres.
mw: Lake Malawi holds more species of fish than any other lake in the world.
my: Malaysian forests grow the rafflesia, the world's largest flower — up to a metre across, and it smells of rotting meat.
na: The Namib is considered the oldest desert on Earth, and its coastal dunes are among the tallest anywhere.
nc: New Caledonia's lagoon is ringed by the second longest coral reef in the world, after the Great Barrier Reef.
ne: Niger is where skeletons of Sarcosuchus were found, giant crocodiles longer than a bus.
ng: Nigeria makes so many films that its industry is nicknamed Nollywood, one of the largest in the world by number of titles.
ni: Nicaragua has a freshwater lake with sharks in it — they swim up the river from the sea.
nl: More than a quarter of the Netherlands lies below sea level, land won back from the water with dikes and pumps.
no: In northern Norway the sun stays up for weeks in summer and never rises for weeks in winter.
Norway's fjords are valleys ploughed out by glaciers and later flooded by the sea.
Skis are older than writing in Norway: a skier was carved on a rock about four thousand years ago.
Almost all of Norway's electricity comes from water falling off the mountains.
Every year Oslo sends London a huge spruce tree as thanks for help during the war.
np: Nepal holds Everest and eight more of the world's fourteen highest peaks.
nz: New Zealand is home to the kiwi, a wingless bird that lays an egg nearly a quarter of its own size.
om: Oman traded frankincense for centuries, shipping the resin of rare trees to Egypt and Rome.
pk: Pakistan has K2, the world's second highest peak and harder to climb than Everest.
pa: The Panama Canal joined two oceans; a ship crosses it in about half a day instead of sailing all the way around South America.
pe: The Inca built Machu Picchu without iron tools, wheels or mortar: the stones fit so tightly you cannot slip a blade between them.
ph: The Philippines is over seven thousand islands, nearly each with its own way of speaking.
pg: Papua New Guinea has nearly 850 languages, more than any other country in the world.
pl: Marie Skłodowska-Curie named the first element she discovered polonium, after Poland.
The salt mine at Wieliczka has worked since the thirteenth century, and a whole chapel with chandeliers is carved from salt.
Nicolaus Copernicus was the first to explain that the Earth goes round the Sun, not the other way about.
In the Bialowieza forest on Poland's border the European bison survives; it was saved after none were left in the wild.
Warsaw's old town was destroyed in the war and then rebuilt from old paintings and drawings.
pr: Puerto Rico has bays that glow at night, lit by tiny organisms that flash when the water moves.
kp: North Korea counts years its own way, starting from the birth of the state's founder.
pt: Portuguese sailors were the first from Europe to reach India around Africa, and Portuguese became a mother tongue on several continents.
Portugal produces more than half the world's cork: the bark is stripped from the oak every nine years and the tree lives on.
The Vasco da Gama bridge in Lisbon runs for more than seventeen kilometres across the Tagus.
Wooden trams still climb the hills of Lisbon: the streets are too steep and narrow for an ordinary bus.
The university at Coimbra opened in 1290 and has been running for more than seven centuries.
py: Almost everyone in Paraguay speaks Guaraní, an indigenous language that is as official as Spanish.
ps: Jericho is considered one of the oldest cities where people have lived without a break for over ten thousand years.
qa: Qatar is a desert peninsula with almost no rivers, but some of the world's largest gas reserves.
ro: Romania has Bran Castle, tied to the Dracula story, though the real prince Vlad hardly ever lived there.
ru: Russia is so wide that it spans eleven time zones: when people go to bed at one end, they are having breakfast at the other.
rw: Rwanda's mountains are home to mountain gorillas, among the rarest large animals on Earth.
eh: Western Sahara is almost entirely desert, with fewer people than live in a single large city.
sa: Saudi Arabia has no permanent rivers at all: its water is either underground or desalinated from the sea.
sd: Sudan has more pyramids than Egypt — around two hundred of them, narrower and more steeply sloped.
ss: South Sudan is the world's youngest country, created in 2011.
sn: Lake Retba near Dakar is so salty that algae living in it turn the water pink.
sb: The Solomon Islands have nurse sharks and saltwater crocodiles, and water so clear you can see the bottom tens of metres down.
sl: Sierra Leone produced one of the largest diamonds ever found, the Star of Sierra Leone, over 900 carats.
sv: El Salvador is called the land of volcanoes: it has a couple of dozen, many visible from the cities.
so: Somalia has the longest coastline of any country on mainland Africa.
rs: Nikola Tesla came from a Serbian family, and the unit of magnetic field strength is named after him.
sr: Suriname is the smallest country in South America, and over nine tenths of it is rainforest.
sk: Slovakia has over a hundred surviving castles — one of the densest collections anywhere for so small a country.
si: Over half of Slovenia is forest, and the word “karst” comes from the Kras region, where such caves were first studied.
se: Sweden gave the world safety matches and the three-point seatbelt, whose patent was handed to everyone for free.
Sweden has a right of public access: you may walk, camp and pick berries in almost any forest, even someone else's.
The Nobel Prizes are awarded in Stockholm; they were founded by the Swede Alfred Nobel, who invented dynamite.
Flat-pack furniture that you take home and assemble yourself was invented in Sweden.
In northern Sweden an ice hotel is built every winter; it melts in spring and is built again in autumn.
sz: Eswatini changed its name in 2018: the old name, Swaziland, was too often confused with Switzerland.
sy: Damascus is among the longest continuously inhabited cities: the streets of its old town have kept their layout for a thousand years.
td: Lake Chad has shrunk many times over in half a century, its shore pulling back by tens of kilometres.
tg: Togo is one of Africa's narrowest countries: a single road runs from the ocean to its northern border.
th: Thailand is the only country in Southeast Asia that was never a European colony.
tj: Mountains cover more than nine tenths of Tajikistan; in the Pamirs the roads climb above four kilometres.
tm: In the Karakum desert a gas crater has burned for over half a century; people call it the door to hell.
tl: Timor-Leste is one of Asia's youngest countries: its independence was recognised in 2002.
tt: Trinidad has a lake of natural asphalt: you can walk on it, and the tar is shipped out for roads around the world.
tn: Desert-planet scenes for Star Wars were filmed in Tunisia, and some of the sets still stand in the sand.
tr: Istanbul sits on two continents at once: part of the city is in Europe, part in Asia, with a strait between them.
tw: Taiwan makes most of the world's most advanced microchips: there is one in almost every phone.
tz: Tanzania has Kilimanjaro, Africa's highest mountain, with snow on its summit almost at the equator.
ug: The Nile, Africa's longest river, flows out of Lake Victoria in Uganda.
ua: Beneath Odesa run catacombs over two thousand kilometres long — the largest network of underground passages in the world.
Ukraine's black earth is among the most fertile soil on the planet; a reference sample was taken to Paris for an exhibition.
A pysanka is a painted egg: the pattern is drawn in hot wax and then dyed, layer after layer.
Arsenalna station on the Kyiv metro lies more than a hundred metres down — no station in the world is deeper.
Western Ukraine keeps the ancient beech forests of the Carpathians, listed as World Heritage.
uy: Uruguay won the very first football World Cup, which it hosted itself in 1930.
us: The current fifty-star design was made by a schoolboy for a class project, and his teacher first gave it a poor grade.
The United States bought Alaska from Russia in 1867 for a little over seven million dollars.
Yellowstone became the first national park in the world when it was created in 1872.
The United States has no official language written into its constitution; English simply took hold.
The river cut the Grand Canyon over millions of years, and its walls show rock nearly two billion years old.
uz: Samarkand and Bukhara stood on the Silk Road, passing silk, paper and glass between China and Europe.
ve: Angel Falls is the highest waterfall in the world: the water drops almost a kilometre and turns to mist on the way.
vn: Nearly two thousand limestone rock islands rise out of the water in Ha Long Bay.
vu: On Pentecost Island men jump from wooden towers with vines tied to their ankles — the custom that bungee jumping grew from.
ye: Yemen's island of Socotra grows dragon's blood trees shaped like open umbrellas, and almost a third of its plants live nowhere else.
za: South Africa has three capitals at once: the government in Pretoria, parliament in Cape Town and the high court in Bloemfontein.
South Africa has more than ten official languages, and its anthem is sung in five of them at once.
Cape Town sits beneath Table Mountain with its flat top, and the cloud spilling over it is called the tablecloth.
The world's first heart transplant was carried out in Cape Town in 1967.
Kruger park is home to the big five: lion, leopard, elephant, rhino and buffalo.
zm: Victoria Falls thunders on Zambia's border; its spray is visible twenty kilometres away, so locals call it the smoke that thunders.
zw: The bird copies carvings found at Great Zimbabwe, an ancient city built of stone without any mortar.
va: Vatican City is the smallest country in the world — under half a square kilometre, entirely inside Rome.
sm: San Marino calls itself the world's oldest republic, founded by tradition in the year 301.
li: Liechtenstein is one of only two countries surrounded entirely by other landlocked countries.
ad: Andorra is ruled jointly by two people — the president of France and a Spanish bishop — an arrangement kept since the 13th century.
mt: Malta has temples older than the Egyptian pyramids, around five and a half thousand years old.
nr: Nauru is the smallest republic in the world; you can drive right around the island in under an hour.
tv: Tuvalu earns money from its internet address .tv, rented by television channels and websites worldwide.
pw: Palau has a lake full of jellyfish that have all but lost their sting: with no predators there, people are allowed to swim in it.
mh: Marshall Islanders made charts from sticks and shells that showed not the islands but the way the waves run.
fm: On Pohnpei stands Nan Madol, a city built across a hundred artificial islets made of stacked basalt logs.
ws: In 2011 Samoa skipped a whole day: the country crossed the date line, so 30 December simply never happened there.
to: Tonga is the only country in Oceania that never lost its independence and is still ruled by a king.
ki: Kiribati stretches across every hemisphere at once, and is among the first places in the world to greet the New Year.
kn: It is the smallest country in the Americas, both by area and by population.
gd: Grenada is called the spice island: its nutmeg even made it onto the flag.
vc: Pirates of the Caribbean was filmed here, and some of the sets still stand on the island.
bb: The trident is broken on purpose: it marks the break with the colonial past.
ag: Antigua is said to have so many beaches that you could swim at a different one every day of the year.
lc: The Pitons rise straight out of the sea: they are the hardened remains of ancient volcanoes.
mv: The Maldives is the flattest country in the world: almost all its land rises less than two metres above the sea.
sc: The Seychelles grows the coco de mer, the largest seed in the world, weighing up to twenty kilograms.
sg: Singapore is a single city with a few islets, and remains one of the world's very few city-states.
bh: Bahrain is an island joined to the mainland by a causeway about 25 kilometres long.
